references_named: Walter Benjamin, The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction (1935)
Jean Tinguely, Homage to New York (1960)
rationale: Strong P1 alignment: the mechanism performs auto-destruction on its own body rather than depicting it — real DOM cells are removed, then the script element removes itself, leaving only the wall label. Metzger is materially new to the catalogue and the Benjamin twist (the web can perform death but never suffer it because of perfect reproducibility) lands as clean double-coding for casual and literate viewers. Tone is dry and cheerfully cynical, ethics and licensing are properly handled, and the self-removing script is an elegant closing gesture that also enacts the auto-destructive premise at the meta-level.
reservations: The script 'self-deletion' removes only the DOM node, not the already-executed code — a reasonable web-native approximation but worth being explicit about. The 30-second lifespan is brisk; the dissolution arc reads more as a quick demo than as the slow ritual Metzger's nylon sheets demanded, and the chance-shuffle happens only once at load, so the visible behaviour per visit is deterministic apart from ordering.
revision_suggestion: Consider a longer lifespan (60–90 s) and a slight progressive acceleration so the dissolution stage reads as matter thinning rather than countdown. Optional: surface a 'resurrect' affordance (a link or hint) in the pre-destruction state so the P7 punchline is set up rather than sprung on the viewer mid-burn; keep the actual resurrection bound to reload to preserve the Benjamin argument.
